Despite this, we were able to turn left base at a normal distance from the runway and execute a touch and go without issue. On the following lap of the pattern, we were number 3 to land, and the downwind leg was stretched 2nm beyond the threshold. As we turned left base, I noted an ADSB track depicting an aircraft joining final from right base with a higher rate of speed. At no point did this aircraft make any position reports. We continued our approach and landing and exited at the first available taxiway. As we turned right to exit the runway both my student and I looked back and to the right to observe our separation from the trailing aircraft. The SR20 (Aircraft Y) passed behind us in the landing attitude with his wheels just touching the ground. Our tail had just cleared the runway and no part of aircraft had passed the runway threshold markings. I estimate that the minimum separation was under 50 feet. Had Aircraft Y made position reports I may have been more aware of our lack of separation and been able to take corrective action in order to avoid this near miss. Had Aircraft Y made an AIM recommended pattern entry he may have been able to better maintain a safe distance from our aircraft and account for the significant closure rate on final approach. Aircraft Y should have executed a go-around once the lack of sufficient separation became clear. Lastly, the presence of a control tower at ZZZ airport would, in my opinion, greatly mitigate the risk of runway incursions and midair collisions.
ASRSN:2127364.s: The pilot and student in an SR20 landed at uncontrolled airport ZZZ while a trailing SR20 (Aircraft Y) failed to report position or execute a go-around. This resulted in a near miss with less than 50 feet of separation as Aircraft Y landed immediately behind them.

ASRSN:2127366.n: I was conducting Flight training in a Cessna 172S when I encountered a NMAC. My student and I were entering ZZZ traffic pattern for Runway XX via a 45 degree entry to the downwind when this event occurred. Another small general aviation aircraft (Aircraft Y) was conducting an over mid field entry into the left downwind for the same runway. Aircraft Y failed to visually scan the downwind and turned right in front of my student and I coming within maybe 300 feet horizontal distance and same exact altitude (1800 MSL - traffic pattern altitude). My student and I took action to remain behind the aircraft that turned into us. I had asked Aircraft Y if they saw the aircraft in the downwind prior to cutting us off and got no response.
ASRSN:2127366.s: A Cessna 172S flight instructor and student encountered a NMAC at 1800 MSL while entering the ZZZ traffic pattern. Another aircraft failed to scan, turned right in front of them at the same altitude within 300 feet, and ignored radio inquiries.

ASRSN:2127376.n: I was pointed south to get a headwind on takeoff. My foreflight with adsb was pointed 'north up.' I did not mentally orient myself considering I was pointed south but my data looked like it was positioned in front of me. The airplane on final looked like it would be coming from my left but was actually coming from my right. They had to do a go around.
ASRSN:2127376.s: The pilot, taking off south with a north-up ADS-B display, misoriented the position of an aircraft on final approach. This spatial disorientation caused the pilot to perceive the traffic incorrectly, resulting in the other aircraft executing a go-around.

ASRSN:2127378.n: I was flying in the ZZZ practice area to practice maneuvers. When the incident occurred, I was at a location near the VFR waypoint ZZZZZ, and was approximately 9 nautical miles from ZZZ. I announced my callsign, location, altitude, direction of flight, and intentions on the appropriate practice area frequency for the altitude I was at. I visually cleared the area and took note of the location of other aircraft that I either saw visually or heard their location over the radio. I did not perceive any conflicting traffic within the area and deemed it safe to commence the maneuver I intended to practice. I began one steep turn. Upon rollout from the turn, I spotted another aircraft that did not appear during my visual scan while clearing the area before the maneuver, flying close to my location, approximately 200 feet above and within close proximity horizontally, roughly 300 feet or less away. Aircraft Y was heading approximately directly towards my aircraft and direction of flight, to the point where I perceived a hazard. I immediately executed a sharp turn to the right to avoid the other aircraft. From what I recall, the other aircraft did not alter its flight direction to avoid the hazard. I did not hear this aircraft make radio calls to other air traffic.Regarding the cause of this event, I feel that it was a lack of awareness on the part of Aircraft Y. I do not believe the other aircraft saw my plane, given that it did not alter its flight path. The absence of radio calls from Aircraft Y did not help the situation. Although radio calls are not a replacement for visual scans, they offer another tool for pilots to use in locating aircraft that may be difficult to see. If an announcement was made, it may have helped both of us avoid each other. However, it is possible that this aircraft may have been making radio calls. The ZZZ practice area has two frequencies to use. One frequency for operations at or below 2,000 feet and another for operations below 4,500 feet. It is possible that this aircraft may have been using the wrong frequency. I cannot say for certain since I was not monitoring the other practice area frequency at the time. This issue comes down to a need for more training regarding situational awareness and use of the radio as a safety tool, which I feel is very important when operating in areas with heavy traffic.
ASRSN:2127378.s: The pilot practicing steep turns in the ZZZ area encountered Aircraft Y, which was 200 feet above and within 300 feet horizontally, requiring an immediate right turn to avoid a collision. The reporter attributed the incident to Aircraft Y's lack of situational awareness and failure to communicate, possibly due to using the wrong practice area frequency.

ASRSN:2127381.n: Directly after take off we had a full power loss between 20-50 feet AGL. We landed immediately, straight ahead on the runway, applied brakes and stopped the aircraft. No damage was done to A/C or runway surface. After landing, the a/c continued to run at idle. While inspecting the aircraft to figure out the problem, the Instructor and I looked at the fuel selector and saw it was selected to the left tank. However, we had taken off with 'both' selected. We decided that, while moving the rudder pedals, my leg pushed the fuel selector in between the 'both' and 'left' detents, and bounced to 'left' on landing. For verification of the issue we taxied back and replicated the issue (with success or failure?). The fuel selector is the Dakota STC fuel selector PN DC11383. The Dakota fuel selector has a large handle that is easy to catch on a body or clothing and creates more leverage than needed. I believe the larger handle is safety issue that can cause fuel starvation in flight.
ASRSN:2127381.s: The pilot and instructor experienced a full power loss between 20-50 feet AGL after takeoff due to the Dakota STC fuel selector (PN DC11383) shifting from 'both' to 'left' when the pilot's leg struck the large handle. They landed safely with no damage, attributing the fuel starvation to the selector's design allowing accidental movement.

ASRSN:2127384.n: IFR flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. I was vfr on top for the whole route of flight. ZZZ1 was reporting 4200 ft. ceilings and 10 miles visibility. About 90 miles to the east of ZZZ1 there was a large opening in the cloud layer so I opted to cancel my IFR and descend below the layer. I made a slow descent to about 700 ft. AGL and saw in front of me that the layer continued to the ground. I initiated a climb away from surrounding terrain and went into IMC. I broke out of the layer again after a few minutes and was able to complete the flight under VFR. In retrospect I should have continued the flight under IFR for longer and most likely been able to cancel closer to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2127384.s: A pilot flying IFR VFR-on-top cancelled the flight plan to descend below clouds but encountered terrain and entered IMC at 700 ft AGL. The pilot climbed out of the layer to complete the flight VFR, noting in retrospect that maintaining IFR longer would have been safer.

ASRSN:2127385.n: On the takeoff roll, I noticed a mower appear from behind hangars on the east side of the runway moving toward the runway. The mower was moving rapidly. The mower entered the runway as I was lifting off the runway, about 100ft ahead of me. I flew over the mower by about 15 feet. As I flew over him, the mower appeared to see me, and swerved back into the grassy runway safety area.There was no chance that I would have been able to stop the plane in time for the mower had I aborted the takeoff, and that's why I decided to continue with the takeoff. It happened very quickly, and the only safe option was to takeoff. I recommend the FAA review the current runway safety practices for ground vehicles at 8W2 airport.
ASRSN:2127385.s: A pilot reported that during takeoff at 8W2, a rapidly moving mower entered the runway just as the aircraft lifted off, passing approximately 15 feet below. The pilot continued the takeoff as aborting was impossible, noting the mower swerved back into the safety area after the aircraft passed.

ASRSN:2127391.n: I did not fully understand that the 400 feet AGL rule applies to all drones. I also believed that my drone was under 0.55 lbs, since this is how it was advertised online on the page from which I purchased my specific configuration.
ASRSN:2127391.s: A drone operator reported misunderstanding the 400 feet AGL rule and incorrectly believing their drone weighed under 0.55 lbs based on online advertising. This led to a potential regulatory violation due to the operator's lack of knowledge regarding weight and altitude restrictions.

ASRSN:2127398.n: Aircraft X departed SAF runway 02 under IFR clearance. Flight plan route SF.V263.ZZZ..ZZZ, climbing to 100. the pilot checked in on the frequency saying they are flying runway heading. I asked the pilot to verify that they are flying runway heading, and not flying any form of departure procedure. Pilot verified, and I issued the climb initially to 110, then to 140. With the aircraft being high-performance jet, the pilot was able to avoid entering the next MIA block below the altitude, albeit barely. As soon as the aircraft left 110 I issued the vector to avoid the upcoming 140 block. The aircraft exited out of the high terrain, and was cleared on course to ZZZ. Suggestion: Although it is relatively rare occurrence, pilots seldom check in on frequency departing SAF flying runway heading. On the runways 33 and 20, it is often non-issue, and the course corrections can be made before any imminent situation. However, aircraft departing runway 02 flying runway heading causes imminent situation as the terrain climbs rapidly. In this instance, the aircraft in question was a very high-performance jet, and the communication was not an issue allowing the situation to be resolved. If the aircraft involved was a low-performance propeller driven, or the communication was an issue, the situation could have been fatal. The fact that this is a recurring issue, the way the aircraft are cleared from SAF ATCT has to address and emphasize how to join SID or to proceed on-course away from high terrain.
ASRSN:2127398.s: An ATC controller and pilot of a high-performance jet departing SAF runway 02 under IFR faced an imminent terrain conflict while flying runway heading. The controller issued vectors to avoid restricted blocks, resolving the situation only because the aircraft's performance allowed it to clear high terrain before entering the next block.

ASRSN:2127462.n: Gate was XX. We were ready to push back, and all checklists were complete. They didn't have a tug/tron available at the time, so we were running about 10 minutes behind schedule. Once the ramp got one and hooked it up, we followed the standard SOP call to flight deck to ramp to make sure everything was ready to go. I noticed too while they were bringing the tron over it was more the style of where it picks you up without the straps, so I knew to suspect hardly any movement once the brake was released. Once the parking brake was released, we started rolling backwards at an alarming rate. I reached up to turn the HYD SYS 1 and 2 to on to get the brakes to work without having to use the parking brake lever. During all this time the ramper had said nothing. Once I reset the parking brake I had asked him if everything was done right since we moved so much. He didn't have much of any response other than 'I forgot the switch'. At that time, I had asked for Operations to watch the footage since they had a camera on us and confirmed that it was moving freely and not connected. I asked for a different tug driver just to have a fresh mind pushing us back and not thinking of what just happened. The ramp manager came over and asked what happened. I had explained everything I could. I'm not sure he understood what had happened because he didn't seem to care too much. I had sent a a message to the station manager. After about 15-20 minutes we had a new tug driver and was able to push back in ZZZ.Cause: I can think of the ramper being told by a higher up at the station just go get an out time and we'll get the rest. Being rushed/being behind. Suggestions: Don't stress being late. I understand the whole short staffed/not having enough equipment to do the job can cause a lot on just try to get an out time since we were already delayed. Being better trained on the equipment you use.
ASRSN:2127462.s: The pilot reported that during pushback at Gate XX, the aircraft rolled backward rapidly because the ramp agent failed to connect the tug properly. The agent admitted forgetting to engage the switch, causing a delay until a new driver arrived to complete the pushback.

ASRSN:2127477.n: While flying the RNAV Y XX aircraft did not intercept the inbound course. Flying pilot disconnected the auto pilot and turned to re-intercept the inbound. ATC inquired and the Pilot flying elected to go around. We then came around and attempted the Localizer XX approach. The Flying pilot didn't initiate a descent to the next lower altitude. He then disconnected the auto pilot to descend. We overshot the next lower altitude and set off a terrain warning to ATC. They inquired and I replied that we were now VMC and had the runway environment in sight. We landed with no further incidence.Suggestions: It was a very short leg and I was very compressed. We initially had the Localizer XX approach selected. ATC said we could shoot either so we decided to input the RNAV Y XX. I suspect I may have loaded the one on top of the other. Then when we didn't intercept, we again loaded the Localizer again. This time mine appeared to load correctly but the fling pilots didn't. We corrected his and continued into VMC conditions and landed. I think as I gain more proficiency in this aircraft, I will be able to better troubleshoot procedural errors as such.
ASRSN:2127477.s: During an RNAV Y approach, the crew failed to intercept the inbound course and elected to go around. While attempting a subsequent Localizer approach, the pilot flying missed a descent step, causing an altitude overshoot and terrain warning before landing safely in VMC.

ASRSN:2127483.n: Rejected takeoff below 80kts for master caution, window heat. Exited runway ran checklists, consulted dispatch and mx. System working as designed. Ran brake cooling and confirmed numbers with dispatch, MX, and PIC agreed to takeoff again37 degree temperature and supplementary procedure completed, but master caution still illuminated before 80kts. This is an ongoing issue with 737 aircraft where the master caution light may illuminate during takeoff even after completing the supplementary procedure for the window heat. It was 38-40 degrees Celsius in ZZZ and 10 minutes prior to take off the crew turned on the window heat and after a short period all the window OFF lights illuminated. The supplemental power test procedure was conducted which cleared the OFF lights as the system was working correctly. A very short time later the crew was cleared for takeoff and prior to the PM 80 knot call the Master Caution illuminated for the windows again and the Captain rejected. In hot conditions with the system working correctly we need a procedure that would allow us to takeoff. We are lucky it didn't happen again and again making it impossible to depart should we follow our reject criteria.
ASRSN:2127483.s: The crew rejected takeoff below 80 knots on a Boeing 737 due to a master caution for window heat in hot conditions. Although the system was working correctly, the light illuminated again despite completing the supplementary procedure, highlighting a need for revised takeoff criteria.

ASRSN:2127515.n: At top of decent we briefed and reviewed approach. After established on RNAVZ 30 we received FINAL APP" and set missed approach altitude. While configuring the airplane for the landing phase we noticed the path was possibly lower than what was published, before we had time to react ATC was already alerting us of low altitude. We were at 5,500 feet and immediately stopped the decent and approach. We then climbed to 6,200 feet and rejoined the approach. We maintained 6200 until back established on the approach then descending to cross SAXIE at 4500 feet. We were stable by SAXIE continuing the approach and landed uneventful. Cause: Fatigue, delayed, not clearly labeled on the approach plate, airplane creating its own path disregarding the published altitudes.Suggestion: Have the altitude labeled on the chart vs lightly labeled on a line between points."
ASRSN:2127515.s: The flight crew descended below the published path on the RNAVZ 30 approach, triggering a low altitude alert at 5,500 feet. They attributed the deviation to fatigue, unclear chart labeling, and the aircraft's flight path logic, but recovered and landed uneventfully after climbing to 6,200 feet.

ASRSN:2127530.n: Previous crew wrote up stall fail caution and did not contact MX. I contacted Mx and asked about the time frame for RTS and decided to board. With passengers on board Mx preformed stall test and it shut down the apu with passengers on board. We then restarted the airplane and MX preformed stall test again with out incident and I informed the passengers that due to a Mx issue from previous flight we had shut the plane down. Mx then returned the plane to service and we completed required tasks and pushed off gate without issue. On taxi out we got hydraulic 3 low pres and hydraulic system 3 high temp and steering inop. We ran associated QHR's and contacted Mx. they informed us we needed to be towed back to gate. Tow team informed us that we were leaking hydraulic fluid and the airport equipment was dispatched to us. Mx then cleared us to be towed and we were towed back to gate. Cause: Potential contributing factor would be improper shutdown while maintenance doing stall test while passengers were on board. Suggestions: Better coordination between crew and Mx regarding non standard shutdown/ termination of aircraft and potential ramifications of this.
ASRSN:2127530.s: The crew and maintenance performed a stall test with passengers on board, causing an APU shutdown, followed by hydraulic system 3 failures and steering inop on taxi. The aircraft was towed back to the gate due to fluid leaks, attributed to improper shutdown coordination during the maintenance test.

ASRSN:2127550.n: We were getting ready for an on time push back at ZZZ. Before we called for push a ground crew member said that there were two extra company boxes that were going to be placed in the forward baggage compartment of the plane. We asked him how much they weighed and then added the weight to the flight. The ground crew gave no indication that there was anything in either box that would not be allowed on the flight. Furthermore, since this was not an unusual occurrence. We simply said 'thank you', 'how much do they weigh' and moved on with the pushback. The next day the Captain got a call that one or both of the boxes contained radio active material and was not allowed on the aircraft. This was the first time that we were informed of this. Had the ground crew alerted us that the boxes contained radio active materials we would have refused them. In the future I will make sure and question the ground crew about any last minute boxes that arrive just prior to pushback. Aircraft was parked in ZZZ airport, ready for pushback for a flight to ZZZ1 airport. Just prior to commencing pushback, the ground crew advises that 2 packages will be loaded onto the aircraft. The forward cargo door was opened and the additional cargo was loaded. After this occurred, CA queried the ground crew asking the weight of the additional cargo as it seemed the ground crew were not able to send this information via the automatic system. After a few minutes, the ground crew advised that each package was 2 pounds. No other information was provided. After modifying the load sheet, new takeoff data was obtained, pushback commenced, with the remainder of the flight being uneventful. The following day, the CA was advised that a report was received indicating that the cargo loaded onto this flight was potentially a Class 7 hazardous material, which is in clear violation of the hazardous materials program, as this is not accepted for transport on aircraft. Had this information been presented by the ground crew during the loading of the cargo, these items would have not been accepted.
ASRSN:2127550.s: The flight crew accepted two unmarked boxes from ground crew during pushback preparation at ZZZ airport after only confirming their weight. The next day, the crew learned the boxes contained radioactive material, a Class 7 hazardous substance prohibited on aircraft, which would have been refused had the ground crew disclosed the contents.

ASRSN:2127557.n: Last night taxiing into CRW we pulled up to the gate adjacent to the ramp area still on the taxiway. The Captain went to maneuver the airplane towards the line so we could pull straight into the gate. During this time the ramp crew did have the X signal with their wands signaling to us that it was not safe to pull into the gate which we saw the entire time. We stopped once we maneuvered the aircraft on the taxiway and waited for the ramp crews to give us the signal to taxi in to park which we did safely and uneventfully. After parking I went down to conduct my postflight walkaround inspection and was met by the Ramp Supervisor. She raised her voice at me and was extremely emotional stating we did not respect their X signal to stop. She raised her voice at me and said something along the lines of are you guys kidding me!? When the X is up you stop! I could file a report on you guys." She was very confrontational. I calmly apologized and stated we were just getting maneuvered into position to pull in once they gave us the go and that I would express her concerns with the Captain which I did immediately. We both felt we were still on the taxiway and we were just maneuvering to get the airplane in position to taxi in to the gate. We talked with ramp crew while at the gate leaving CRW the next day around XA:00 and they showed us the line that separates taxiway from ramp area. We agreed that the Captain did cross the line before stopping which he took full ownership of. We stopped shortly after making the turn and we did not see anything that would have been unsafe.The root cause was a combination of dark taxiway, ramp area, awkward gate setup, and a miscommunication of procedures between this particular Ramp Supervisor and us the pilots who were just looking to get into a better position to actually pull into the gate once the crew did give us the signal to continue. We did not see the particular line which is where the ramp begins.The taxiway and ramp areas around the gate are very dark. The line that we crossed is very difficult to see at night. The gate is also on an awkward angle when pulling in which is why we maneuvered before stopping. Suggestion would be better lighting around the ramp and maybe a section in the company pages to alert crews of this if it is indeed something that becomes an issue." As we were taxiing toward the gate area at CRW, the three marshallers appeared to be in place but had the lighted wands up in 'X'. This is very common when they aren't ready for us to taxi into the gate. This particular gate was at a blind sharp angle. To make for a better line-up position, I slowly pulled forward of the line-up line. As I turned to the right, toward the line, the 'X' was still in place, so I stopped the aircraft mid-turn. We were visibly clear of all obstacles, and I was positioning the aircraft with the intent to stop once properly lined up. We were still outside the 'box'. After I stopped the aircraft, the marshallers signaled to continue, and we were brought into the gate without incident. The supervisor approached the FO on his walkaround and began yelling at him in an unprofessional manner. He politely apologized and stated that we were just lining up the aircraft and had no intent to park ourselves with the 'X' up, but that we were going to stop once the nose was in position. She appeared to take personal offense to all of this, even though we were outside the box, so we decided to submit this report.I had a supervisor walk me out on the ramp to Spot C1 to get a good look at it during daylight. There was a black dotted line, just to the inside of the taxi line, that I maneuvered inside of while I was in my turn to the right, for the angled gate. At night, the lineup line, as well as that dotted line, were difficult to see. It is my recommendation that the ramp at CRW be better lit at night. If I had seen that black dotted line, I would have stopped the aircraft outside it.
ASRSN:2127557.s: Pilots at CRW crossed a faint ramp line while maneuvering an aircraft into a blind, angled gate at night, stopping immediately upon seeing the ramp crew's 'X' signal. A confrontational supervisor accused them of ignoring the signal, though the pilots attributed the incident to poor lighting, an awkward gate setup, and a misunderstanding of the specific line location.

ASRSN:2127560.n: We were departing runway 18R when we encountered severe wake/shear behind an A321 at around 800ft. The YD (Yaw Damper) automatically kicked off and we got a stick shaker for less than 1 second. The PF began losing control of the aircraft, I took the wheel but by then it was basically over. I turned to a heading of 310 and continued the climb, we did the after takeoff checklist and I handed the aircraft back to the FO.Suggestion: We were still in ATTCS (Automatic Takeoff Thrust Control System) mode, PF didn't go into T/O-1 mode. No fault to him, but we should implement a training procedure where we treat wake turbulence as a windshear escape maneuver. We taxied to rwy 18R and departed behind an A320 series. As we were cleared for take-off, the A320 had just rotated off 18R. I remember thinking, 'This is really tight.' I was pilot flying and performed a normal takeoff to roughly 1,000, and that's when we encountered wake turbulence. The plane immediately banked roughly 30 right then 30-45 left, which caused the autopilot to turn off. The Captain took control of the airplane and the stick shaker began to sound momentarily. The plane began to stabilize and we continued our takeoff profile and checked in with ATC. We landed without further incident.Cause: Wake turbulence was the root cause of the problem. Suggestion: We also could have delayed our takeoff. ATC should have provided more spacing between us and the A320.
ASRSN:2127560.s: Pilots departing runway 18R behind an A320 encountered severe wake turbulence at 1,000ft, causing autopilot disengagement, a momentary stick shaker, and significant bank angles. The Captain took control to stabilize the aircraft, which continued the climb and landed safely, with the reporter citing wake turbulence and insufficient ATC spacing as causes.

ASRSN:2127659.n: While instructing an instrument student we descended below mda and were a little left of our course. We corrected but I the instructor should have corrected my students actions in a more timely manner.
ASRSN:2127659.s: An instructor and student descended below the minimum descent altitude and drifted left of course during an instrument training flight. The instructor attributed the incident to a failure to correct the student's actions in a timely manner.

ASRSN:2127678.n: While on a training flight with a newer student with less than 5 hours, I had him simulate a engine-out descent near ZZZ. Amongst many other maneuvers executed on that flight, this one was going well. I had him set up as if he was going to land in the field he had chosen. We were in a sparsely populated area with no structures, persons, or vessels around. When confirming the landing would have been executed properly the student pilot went full power and executed a 'go around' to climb back to altitude where we would debrief the maneuver. After the flight I glanced at my Garmin and realized how close to the ground we got. According to my elevation map the student recovered at around 300 AGL in a sparsely populated area. Although the law is to stay 500FT away from persons/structures/ and vessels I believe that was still achieved. However, I learned it is not necessary to recover this low to teach the student about the engine out decent.
ASRSN:2127678.s: During a training flight with a student pilot, an engine-out descent simulation near ZZZ resulted in a go-around recovery at approximately 300 feet AGL. The instructor noted that while no persons or structures were violated, the low recovery altitude was unnecessary for the training objective.

ASRSN:2127680.n: Upon landing on Runway 29, I mistook a perpendicular, crossing Runway 02-20 as Taxiway G. The markings of the exit to Taxiway A off of Runway 02-20 led me to this confusion.
ASRSN:2127680.s: The pilot mistook crossing Runway 02-20 for Taxiway G while landing on Runway 29. This confusion was caused by the markings of the exit to Taxiway A off Runway 02-20.

ASRSN:2127700.n: During roll out from landing, nose gear collapsed. This was first flight after Annual inspection. The annual included removal and replacement of almost everything in the hydraulic system. Cause of nose gear collapse was found to be improper rigging of nose gear over center lock.I believe my preflight and inflight checks were sound with no apparent indications available to me, the pilot, of the impending collapse. However, I also believe there are some risk management mitigations that I will add to improve my procedures in the future. First, next time I fly an airplane just out of major maintenance, I will pull 2 to 2 1/2 G's once I have lowered the gear. This will allow the 'extra' weight of the gear to perhaps lower the gear slightly further and prevent collapse. Second, I read an article in last 6 months claiming that for small general aviation aircraft, if the alternator is not at full capacity on basically all brands of General Aviation retractable gear airplanes, then the gear may not fully extend. So, I am now adding to my procedures that every time I check gear down green lights that I will also check the ammeter for any large deflection. If a large ammeter deflection is occurring and there are no other indications, then I will pull added g's in an attempt to complete gear lowering to its full extent. I will also ask the tower to observe my landing gear positioning after this maneuver as an added precaution.Finally, it occurred to me in hind sight that I know a very good mechanic with 12 year's experience on retractable gear Cessna Cardinals and has experienced this circumstance. From now on, whenever I fly an airplane fresh out of major maintenance, I will seek advice from someone experienced in the particular type of maintenance issue for any additional advice.
ASRSN:2127700.s: The pilot reported a nose gear collapse during rollout after landing on the first flight following an annual inspection involving hydraulic system work. The cause was identified as improper rigging of the nose gear over-center lock, with no preflight or inflight indications available to the pilot.

ASRSN:2127705.n: I was repositioning my airplane from the one ramp to another for a flight. I received my taxi instructions to hold short of the active runway. I read back my clearance and complied. I was instructed to monitor the Tower frequency so I did. Tower instructed me to cross Runway XX, right at [Taxiway] 1, and exit on [Taxiway] 2. I read back my clearance and rolled past the hold short line. I looked both ways before crossing the runway and saw an Archer on short final. I stopped before the runway markings, but past the hold short line to query ATC. ATC sent the other plane to go around and told me to expedite my crossing. They said they had notified me of the airplane on final. I read back the instruction and cleared the runway. I did not receive a phone number for a possible pilot deviation. I believe I should have queried ATC before accepting my clearance and crossing the hold short line. My perception of aircraft spacing lead me to stopping, however, I should have complied with the clearance and expedited my runway crossing. Alternately, I should have remained behind the hold short line and responded 'unable' to the instructions.
ASRSN:2127705.s: The pilot crossed the hold short line while taxiing to cross Runway XX after seeing an Archer on short final. The pilot stopped to query ATC, who sent the Archer around and instructed an expedited crossing, though the pilot admitted they should have queried before crossing or responded "unable."

ASRSN:2127752.n: On final descent into ZZZ we were told to expect moderate turbulence from 17k to the ground. Flight Attendant's (FAs) were seated prior to top of descent because we knew it might be bumpy. Turbulence was moderate from 17k to 12k. Around 12k, the aircraft became uncontrollable at times and the autopilot disengaged itself. I requested with ATC an unrestricted descent to 6k. The CA was pilot flying and it was so turbulent that he had to maintain both hands on the yoke for control. I recall looking up at the Primary Flight Display (PFD) and seeing 8,800 ft. and 290 kts. When the turbulence finally lighted up at 4k in the downwind, I reported the previous severe turbulence to ATC.
ASRSN:2127752.s: During final descent into ZZZ, the crew encountered severe turbulence below 12,000 feet that caused autopilot disengagement and required the Captain to manually control the aircraft at 290 knots. The pilot requested an unrestricted descent to 6,000 feet and reported the severe conditions to ATC once turbulence lightened at 4,000 feet.

ASRSN:2127776.n: On arrival from the ZZZZZ arrival to the ILS XX into ZZZ we were inside of ZZZZZ1 and were given a frequency change to another Approach Control frequency. We had either copied the frequency wrong or given the wrong frequency and told to return to the last frequency. This happened twice and while were working this out we had to remain at our last cleared altitude of 6000. Once we got the frequency issue worked out we were high and needed to descend to the approach intercept altitude. Our clearance was to maintain 210 kts. and above 2000 until established and cleared for the ILS XX approach. As we had already intercepted the Localizer and were inside the IAF I armed the approach mode and commanded the FO to set 1500 in the altitude window of the Mode Control Panel (MCP), the final approach fix altitude and the MCP to flight level change 210 kts trying to catch up on our higher than normal intercept on the approach. At that time I was expecting the aircraft to level off at 2000 until intercepting the glide slope as it was the next altitude at the ZZZZZ2 fix on the approach. The aircraft proceeded to descend to 1500 the set final approach fix altitude without leveling at the 2000 ZZZZZ2 altitude. I didn't catch that mistake and believed we were okay to descend to the 1500 FAF altitude to intercept the glide slope. Approaching 1600 msl (400 low) we received a call from the Approach Controller stating that we got a low altitude alert as we were below the minimum altitude for ZZZZZ2 and to climb back to 2000. We did as requested and were subsequently re-cleared for the approach and landed without incident.
ASRSN:2127776.s: The flight crew experienced frequency issues and descended below the 2000-foot minimum at the ZZZZZ2 fix while intercepting the ILS XX approach. This occurred because the pilot set the MCP to 1500 feet instead of 2000, triggering a low altitude alert that required a climb before a safe landing.

ASRSN:2127869.n: I am on my second Operational Evaluation (OE) flight. I was pilot flying. About 2 hours en-route to ZZZ, all of sudden saw a flashing light outside of window. Then we started to feel severe turbulence. Autopilot got disconnected. Captain took over the control. We stalled at one point and lost about 5000 feet. After couple minutes, Captain finally gained the aircraft control back to the desire position.Cause: Possibility of improper use of radar.Suggestions: Be vigilant especially knowing the weather we will encounter.
ASRSN:2127869.s: During an Operational Evaluation flight en-route to ZZZ, the pilot flying encountered severe turbulence and a flashing light, causing autopilot disconnect, a stall, and a 5,000-foot altitude loss. The captain regained control, and the reporter attributed the incident to possible improper radar use.

ASRSN:2127876.n: Inbound MIA filed FROGZ4 MARCI transition. Given direct KLEET which is on GAWKS transition. We started to get busy at this point while bouncing in and out of cumulonimbus build ups. Switched over to Approach and were told expect visual 8L. We had planned Runway 9 as is usually the case from this arrival. I told the First Officer (FO) I would set us up for that since we were bouncing around pretty good and he had his hands full with misc. ATC instructions like change in airspeeds. As soon as I was done reprogramming the FMC and aircraft for the RNAV 8L, ATC switched us back to ILS 9. This caused a hurry as we were approaching LLEGG intersection which changes the arrival. The ATC instructions were to proceed to LLEGG and intercept localizer. This created a higher altitude situation and the FO was trying his best to get down and slow down per ATC instructions. In this situation we were down going down the glide slope and trying to slow down asap. FO was calling for flaps and gear as needed and called for flaps 15' at 208 kts. (200 max) and since I was finishing up FMC HUD check, I just reached over and selected the flaps from 5' to 15'. I immediately knew what I had done and returned the flap lever to 5'. I don't think the lever was in the 15' slot for more than 1-2 seconds. Flew rest of approach without incident under stable approach criteria.Cause: We got task saturated in busy airspace and rough ride conditions, therefore I got ahead of company procedures to look and say speed verified.Suggestions: Strict adherence to company SOP. ATC send us direct KLEET for the FROGZ4 arrival for Runway 8L RNAV all of a sudden they told us to expect Runway 9 we were high and they told us to slow down which did not help we exceeded the flaps 15 speed 8 kts. faster at 208 kts. next time I would ask for vectors to avoid the mistake that I did for asking for flaps 15 my Captain put the flaps back to flaps 10 in 1 second when he realized that we where 208 kts. we contacted Maintenance and reported I will be more careful in the future. Cause: We where in rough air and were cought in the wake turbulence from an aircraft in front of us and ATC giving us a last minute change of runway which ultimately played in beeing behind on a stable approach it was my mitake to accept the last minute change of runway.Suggestions: I would not accept the approach and ask for vectors to not be in a rush.
ASRSN:2127876.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced task saturation during a rough approach to MIA after ATC issued a last-minute runway change from 8L to 9. The Captain inadvertently selected flaps 15 at 208 knots, exceeding the limit, but immediately corrected the error and completed a stable approach.

ASRSN:2127907.n: Approximately an hour into flight at FL330, we received a Level 1-Tank 1 and 3, Tip Fuel Low warning. About 15 mins later, received a Level 2-Fuel Qty/Used Chk warning. Calculated total Fuel used plus FOB, estimated over 10,000# of fuel missing. Diverted to ZZZ. [Priority handling requested] to have crash rescue ensure no fuel visibly leaking to the ground after landing. Taxied to gate with no further incident. Cause: Aircraft maintenance Approximately one hour into the flight, received level 1 TANK 3 TIP FUEL LO" and "TANK 1 TIP FUEL LO" alerts. Soon after, we received a "FUEL QTY/USED CHK" level 2 alert and a "POSSIBLE FUEL LEAK" message. We complied with the QRH and were unable account for approximately 10,000 lbs of fuel. The Captain coordinated with Dispatch and we opted to divert to ZZZ. We [requested priority handling] and asked for Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) to meet us upon landing to determine if there was a visible fuel leak. No fuel leak was observed. We taxied to the gate uneventfully. Cause: Aircraft maintenance"
ASRSN:2127907.s: The flight crew encountered fuel low warnings and a possible leak message at FL330, estimating 10,000 lbs of missing fuel. They diverted to ZZZ with priority handling and CFR standby, landing safely with no visible leak; the cause was attributed to aircraft maintenance.

ASRSN:2127919.n: We were coming into LGA at night and we got descended from 10 to 8k. The aircraft in front of of us either didn't get the descent or was slow to descend and we started getting bounced around from their wake. When we asked to be vectored out of his wake they gave us a 90dg turn and seemed like they were vectoring us off the arrival and were putting us in the back of the arrival line. So, we clarified and said we just need vectored out of the wake. The controller corrected and gave us a new heading. The new heading took us closer to the city than the traffic ahead of us. We got a another descent from 8 to 4k and we were advised of a helicopter at our 1 o'clock at 4.5k circling over the city. I don't know if it was cause we were on a different heading than the plane in front but the vector seemed to be taking us close but we had them in sight. The helicopter looked to be turning away from us but circled back to us. Frequency was busy and we couldn't ask for anything so I (pilot flying (PF)) turned a few more degrees away from the traffic trying to avoid a RA. We received an RA so I kicked off the Autopilot followed the RA guidance and First Officer (FO) told ATC we were responding to an RA. Once maneuver was complete we turned Autopilot back on and continued being vectored for the approach.
ASRSN:2127919.s: During a night arrival at LGA, the crew encountered wake turbulence and received a vector that placed them near a circling helicopter. The pilot manually deviated to avoid a Traffic Alert, but an RA was still triggered, requiring autopilot disengagement to follow resolution guidance before rejoining the approach.

ASRSN:2127924.n: We were getting vectored for the ILS 22 in to AVP. We were in IMC condition. ATC told us to decent down to 3700 ft after reaching 3700 ft and flying on the assigned heading of 300 we received a terrain warning so I disconnected the auto pilot and climbed. We ended up climbing to 4600 ft and advised ATC about the terrain warning. ATC said the vectoring altitude was 3700 ft in the area and gave us a decent back to 4000 ft and a heading of 250 to re-clear us for the ILS 22 in to AVP. We had a normal landing to complete our flight at AVP.
ASRSN:2127924.s: While being vectored for ILS 22 at AVP in IMC, the crew received a terrain warning after descending to 3,700 ft on heading 300. The pilot disconnected the autopilot and climbed to 4,600 ft, then descended to 4,000 ft on a new heading to complete a normal landing.

ASRSN:2127954.n: On departure out of IND, and while level at 3000 feet, witnessed what appeared to be a small drone pass about 1/4 mile off our right wing. Drone appeared to be small in nature and fairly flat in shape but made lateral movements that appeared to meet the characteristics of a drone. No evasive action was necessary but report was made to ATC as it was about 2500-2800 feet and in side the class Charlie airspace.
ASRSN:2127954.s: A pilot reported a small, flat drone passing 1/4 mile off the right wing at 3,000 feet during departure from IND. No evasive action was required, but the pilot notified ATC as the drone was within Class Charlie airspace at 2,500–2,800 feet.

ASRSN:2127955.n: During flight at 2500 MSL within five miles of ZZZ I spotted a drone approximately 300 ft. Below our left wing. The drone passed and I was not able to track its course as we headed away from IND on ATC vectors. It appeared approximately one to two feet in diameter with a single prop and I alerted ATC as we left their airspace.
ASRSN:2127955.s: A pilot reported spotting a single-prop drone approximately 300 feet below the left wing while flying at 2,500 feet MSL near ZZZ. The drone passed out of sight as the aircraft departed on ATC vectors, and the pilot alerted air traffic control upon leaving their airspace.

ASRSN:2127982.n: Was performing eights on pylons with student. We did a 180 degree clearing turn and began the maneuver after not seeing anyone. After completing the second pylon, we saw a crop duster flying within 1,000 feet of us off our right wingtip. Began climbing up immediately when noticed. Crop duster did not have ADSB. Potential NMAC.
ASRSN:2127982.s: A pilot and student performing eights on pylons encountered a crop duster within 1,000 feet off the right wingtip after a clearing turn. The pilot climbed immediately to avoid a potential NMAC, noting the crop duster lacked ADSB.

ASRSN:2127993.n: Engine roughness and spike in RPMs forced aircraft to [request priority handling] and return to airport. Aircraft RPM's oscillating +/- 300 RPM's and passengers experienced sensation similar to buffeting in climb out. Communicated with tower and made a right turn to land on Runway XX.
ASRSN:2127993.s: The pilot reported engine roughness and RPM oscillations of +/- 300 during climb out, causing a buffeting sensation for passengers. This forced a priority return to the airport, where the aircraft executed a right turn to land on Runway XX.

ASRSN:2127995.n: While maneuvering in the practice area we experienced a Dual ECU failure in flight. The annunciation cleared a few seconds later but this was followed by a partial power loss. There was no vibration or roughness however there was an abnormal ticking noise. With the throttle set at max the load would come up to ~60% them extremely slowly go up to ~80%. It would NOT go any higher than that. We then decided to divert to ZZZ. Upon landing at ZZZ 2 available power checks were done. Both with the same result. With the throttle at full the load would NOT go above 71% power and a dual ECU failure was triggered. The aircraft was then shut down until maintenance could inspect the aircraft.
ASRSN:2127995.s: Pilots experienced a dual ECU failure and partial power loss capped at 71% during practice maneuvers, accompanied by an abnormal ticking noise. They diverted to ZZZ, where post-landing checks confirmed the power limitation and ECU fault, resulting in the aircraft being shut down for maintenance inspection.

ASRSN:2128004.n: Took off runway XXR at ZZZ. At around 800 feet during a left turn to the east we experienced engine roughness at 100% power. Upon reducing the power from 100% to ~90% the roughness did not subside. After reducing the power further to ~75% the roughness subsided. Engine stayed stable after that and resulted in a safe landing on runway XY at ZZZ.
ASRSN:2128004.s: The pilot reported engine roughness at 100% power during a left turn at 800 feet after takeoff from runway XXR at ZZZ. Reducing power to approximately 75% stabilized the engine, allowing for a safe landing on runway XY at ZZZ.

ASRSN:2128025.n: In traffic pattern at ZZZ on downwind and a non-ADSB Blue/white Decathalon crossed at TPA where turn base-final for [Runway] XX. No comms, SP (Student Pilot) deviated pattern to avoid conflict. IP (Instructor Pilot) attempted to hail aircraft. No response. Near Mid Air Collision (NMAC)
ASRSN:2128025.s: A Student Pilot and Instructor Pilot flying in the traffic pattern at ZZZ deviated to avoid a non-ADSB Decathalon crossing at TPA. The unresponsive Decathalon caused a near mid-air collision while the student turned base-final for Runway XX.

ASRSN:2128057.n: While established on the left crosswind for Runway XX at ZZZ, another company aircraft made their initial inbound call at just 3 nm to the east of the airport. The student pilot, later discovered to be on a stage check, proclaimed he was planning for a midfield cross to the opposing runway (Runway XX). Immediately upon hearing the call, I (instructor pilot in the twin) made a radio call that the winds were heavily favoring Runway XY and we were already established in the pattern but did not have them in sight. The student in the approaching aircraft proceeded to make a radio call stating they had us in sight and were going to change to enter the 45 to the downwind we were at this point already on. The other aircraft then continued descend into us and made no turn to for their proposed entry. Not having them in sight, my student descended below pattern altitude where he caught glimpse of the incoming company plane directly at our 3 o'clock and made a turn to avoid conflict. During this time, we received at TCAS alert on the G1000 indicating just 300 ft. of vertical separation. Once appropriate spacing existed, we continued our pattern with no further problem.
ASRSN:2128057.s: An instructor and student in a twin aircraft on left crosswind for Runway XX at ZZZ encountered a TCAS alert with only 300 ft vertical separation. The conflict occurred when another company aircraft, piloted by a student on a stage check, descended directly toward them without turning for a 45-degree entry despite radio warnings.

ASRSN:2128088.n: After landing on XXR at ZZZ I had little to no authority on the right brake causing the aircraft to veer to the left. The aircraft came to a stop before going onto the grass.
ASRSN:2128088.s: The pilot reported little to no authority on the right brake after landing on runway XXR at ZZZ, causing the aircraft to veer left. The aircraft stopped before entering the grass.

ASRSN:2128116.n: My student and I landed on runway XX at ZZZ [airport]. Once the plane touched down ATC advised us to taxi off on [taxiway] 1, we advised we would comply. Upon reaching [taxiway] 1 my student stepped on the brakes to slow down, at which time the aircraft went to the right and did not slow down. I took immediate controls of the aircraft and confirmed that the left brakes had failed. While still on the runway and after passing taxiway 1, ATC cleared another airplane to takeoff. I immediately notified ATC about the issue at which time ATC canceled the other aircraft's takeoff clearance. I was able to turn the aircraft and taxi safely off the runway. We taxied back to the ramp with no issues and squawked the airplane. Maintenance advised that the brakes were damaged and brought the aircraft into service.
ASRSN:2128116.s: A pilot and student experienced left brake failure while taxiing off the runway after landing, causing the aircraft to veer right. The pilot took control, notified ATC to cancel a conflicting takeoff, and safely taxied to the ramp where maintenance repaired the damaged brakes.

ASRSN:2128140.n: Original plan to fly to ZZZ [airport] for Landings and Maneuvers in the airspace for a refresher flight for a student. After flight lesson elements were completed we climbed to 3500 for the arrival. Upon reaching altitude, performing checklist, and checking in with ATC we realized our RPM's and Load was oscillating from 75% to 85% load. We also began to smell smoke. There was no annunciations or Alerts to advise us something was wrong. Once we identified the abnormalities a positive exchange of flight controls was initiated by the instructing pilot and autopilot was disconnected and the instructing pilot flew the aircraft and handled coms while the student pilot ran the QRC/QRH. We [requested priority handling] with ZZZ ATC and chose to divert to ZZZ since we were approximately 5 nm to the north of the airport. ZZZ ATC approved of this and told us to squawk VFR, frequency change approved and 2 planes in the pattern at ZZZ". Prior to the descent we initiated the engine trouble shooting in flight checklist and upon giving the aircraft max load, we lost about 50% of our power. After identifying the loss of power the instructing pilot realized that the load was not able to sustain power lever changes and when increasing the power we would lose the ability to go back to previous power settings. During the descent down to ZZZ the instructing pilot [advised] on the ZZZ unicom while giving traffic advisories to planes in the pattern. Traffic in the pattern at ZZZ was on the upwind and downwind of Runway XX. They extended both of their legs and allowed us to get in as a priority aircraft. During the descent down we lost positive engine control and the instructing pilot performed a power off (power level was at idle) landing from base to final at approximately 1300 feet msl. Landing was made safely and propeller continued to oscillate fluctuating from 1% load to about 11% with RPMs fluctuating from approximately 500-900. Oil pressure 1.4 and unstable. We were able to taxi and park on a parking tee where we advised traffic at ZZZ we were clear of the runway and attempted to contact ATC, secured the aircraft, and exited the plane as it was smoking badly and in the moment we did not know where the smoke was coming from. Once on the ground we contacted Flight ops and Maintenance. Once Maintenance arrived and did their initial inspection. The belly of the aircraft was covered in oil from gascolator to tail and inside of the cowling the aircraft was virtually clean. Upon further inspection Multiple possible failures were identified with the turbocharger and oil lines."
ASRSN:2128140.s: During a student refresher flight, the instructing pilot and student diverted to ZZZ after experiencing oscillating engine load, smoke, and eventual power loss due to suspected turbocharger and oil line failures. The crew executed a power-off landing at 1300 feet MSL, landing safely before exiting the smoking aircraft for maintenance inspection.

ASRSN:2128146.n: During landing at ZZZ [airport], [runway] XXR in Aircraft X with the student pilot in command, we experienced a loss in right braking authority after touchdown. The aircraft veered left and eventually came to a stop on the runway. We stopped in close proximity to the taxiway R light leading off of the runway. I advised Tower that we were unable to taxi off of the runway as I was not sure if we had enough clearance to clear the taxiway light. Tower diverted landing traffic and sent an Airport Operations vehicle to assist. We exited the plane and maneuvered it by hand past the taxiway light, got back in the aircraft and taxied back to the ramp without issue. It was not immediately clear what caused the loss of right brake authority, however searching the closed squawks for that aircraft revealed that it was not the first occurrence.
ASRSN:2128146.s: A student pilot in Aircraft X experienced right brake failure during landing at ZZZ, causing the aircraft to veer left and stop near a taxiway light. After Tower diverted traffic and sent assistance, the crew manually moved the plane past the light; the brake issue was linked to a recurring fault found in the aircraft's closed squawks.

ASRSN:2128153.n: Aircraft X arrival [runway] XXR, 3500ft. Passing ZZZZZ, Near miss, Aircraft Y, Citation Jet, 300-400 ft below, passing above, less then 1/2 away. No ATC advisory of traffic. Had to take corrective action, altered course, descended to 3100, notified ATC of deviation for traffic. Once determined cleared/ safe, notified ATC of climb back to 3500 and on course for the arrival. ATC reply Roger" and then gave us radar vectors inbound."
ASRSN:2128153.s: Aircraft X, arriving at 3500ft, experienced a near miss with a Citation Jet 300-400ft below due to a lack of ATC traffic advisories. The pilot descended to 3100ft and altered course to avoid the conflict before resuming the arrival after ATC provided radar vectors.

ASRSN:2128154.n: We were completing laps in the pattern at HFY using runway 1. Runway 1 was the active runway in use and there was one other aircraft in the pattern with us. When we were turning from crosswind to downwind, we heard the other aircraft in the pattern cue the radio and state Aircraft departing runway 19, do you have your radio on" and received no response. An aircraft had departed runway 19 (Aircraft Y) straight out with no radio calls when runway 1 was in use. The other aircraft in the traffic pattern was on a left base for runway 1 when (Aircraft Y) departed runway 19 using no radios. We heard on the radio from the other aircraft that they had an NMAC, less then 500 ft of separation due to the aircraft departing runway 19 when runway 1 was in use. We were not involved with the NMAC, we decided to file a report due to being in the traffic pattern at the time of the incident." Took off rwy 1 out of HFY. Was on the downwind when I noticed two planes where close on the MFD. A twin aircraft had taken off rwy 19 out of HFY and almost hit an small aircraft on final for rwy 1. We were in the downwind as it happen. The twin made zero radio calls during the incident and did not respond when the FBO tried to call the twin.
ASRSN:2128154.s: A twin aircraft departed Runway 19 at HFY without radio calls while Runway 1 was active, causing an NMAC with less than 500 feet of separation to a small aircraft on final. The reporting pilots observed the incident from downwind while operating in the pattern.

ASRSN:2128177.n: Flight Lesson out of ZZZ [airport] to ZZZ1 [airport] for landings, then continued on for maneuver work in the airspace. Departed ZZZ at approximately XA:45. Refresher flight for me with my instructor, (IP) on board. After concluding the lesson, set up for the ZZZZZ arrival at 3,500 ft. We completed the climb to 3,500 ft, contacted approach and finished setting up for our arrival. Soon after, we noticed oscillating RPM's and Load. We also noticed a faint smell of smoke. We received no annunciations on our flight display during the entirety of this event. Noticing this, we had a positive exchange of flight controls. The instructor was in charge of flight controls and communications while I ran the appropriate QRH/QRC Checklists. Instructing pilot [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Approach and told them we would be conducting a landing into ZZZ1 [airport]. At this time, we were approximately 5 NM north of the airport. ZZZ Approach advised us to Squawk VFR, Frequency changed approved to ZZZ1, 2 in the pattern". We initiated the Engine Troubleshooting checklist from our QRH. An element of this checklist instructed us to give the aircraft max load. Upon doing this, we lost about 50% engine power. The Instructing pilot noticed this and realized we were unable to reach certain load performance. During this, we began our descent into the ZZZ1 traffic pattern entering on the left downwind for Runway XX. With 2 planes in the pattern, the instructing pilot [advised] on the ZZZ1 Unicom and advised of a priority landing. There was traffic on upwind and downwind, both planes extended these legs to allow us to safely execute our landing. While in the Traffic pattern, we noticed we lost positive engine control and the instructing pilot performed a power off landing. This was conducted on base to final at approximately 1,300 ft MSL. Landing was made safely. Once on the ramp, the propeller continued to oscillate from 1-10% load. RPM's fluctuated from 500-900 and Oil pressure was reading 1.4 and unstable. Once landing was made, we advised clear of the runway on Unicom and attempted to contact ZZZ ATC. Upon parking on the ramp, we began to see the smoke and safely powered down the plane and secured it. We noticed the entire underside of the plane was covered in oil from the engine all the way to the tail. We contacted our Chief Instructors along with the maintenance team."
ASRSN:2128177.s: During a training flight, a pilot and instructor experienced oscillating RPMs, smoke, and eventual total engine power loss while approaching ZZZ1. They executed a safe power-off landing after ATC and other traffic provided priority handling, revealing significant oil leakage post-landing.

ASRSN:2128203.n: During a VFR repositioning flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1, my aircraft experienced a complete engine failure during initial descent into ZZZ1. The aircraft engine had hiccuped" a few times earlier in the flight. So, while an engine failure is never completely expected, I was not overly surprised when it did happen. Because of this suspicion, I chose to flight at a relatively high cruising altitude and overflew airports (ZZZ3, ZZZ4, ZZZ) that were near the direct route to ZZZ1. Just before reaching ZZZ, ZZZ Approach directed me to descend to 2000 ft and fly the ZZZZZ arrival. I initiated the descent and turned directed ZZZZZ. A few minutes later, the engine quit. The propeller was not moving, and I made no attempt to restart the engine. I was approximately 4 NM north of ZZZ at this point, so I trimmed for best glide and turned toward the airport. I notified ZZZ Approach that I'd had an engine failure and intended to land at ZZZ but never declared MAYDAY or squawked 7700. Final approach to was steep but otherwise normal. Landing was made without incident. There was no structural damage to the aircraft or airport, and I was also unhurt. The FBO crew arrived with a Jeep and tow bar. They moved the aircraft from the runway to a tie down near the FBO. It's relevant to mention that this was my fourth flight in the aircraft that day. The first flight at XA:00 was a refresher flight with a check instructor and was without incident. All systems were nominal during that flights preflight. The plane was then refueled using our standard fuel provider at ZZZ1. I again preflighted the aircraft, found everything to be nominal, and flew to ZZZ2 without incident. I was at ZZZ2 for a check ride. After the oral portion of the exam, approximately two hours later, I again preflighted the aircraft and removed approximately 4" of water from the gascolator. The wing tank fuel appeared fine. I pulled an additional sample from the gascolator to assure there wasn't any additional water. During the practical portion of the check ride, just after climb out, the engine "hiccuped" twice. It was enough to give me a bit of pause, but I figured there must have been a bit of remnant water. I quickly let it go as the pressures of the check ride took my attention. After the check ride and debrief, I once again preflighted the airplane and, again everything was nominal. There wasn't water in any of the fuel samples and the aircraft wasn't refueled. However, as stated above, there were several more hiccups during the early portion of the return flight to ZZZ."
ASRSN:2128203.s: The pilot experienced a complete engine failure during VFR descent into ZZZ1, likely caused by fuel contamination after earlier "hiccups" and water removal. The pilot glided to a safe landing at ZZZ without injury or damage, though no MAYDAY was declared.

ASRSN:2128212.n: Engine roughness after take off around 2000 ft. Instructor took over and roughness continued. Reached 4600 ft, called approach to return back to field. Proceeded to land.
ASRSN:2128212.s: The pilot reported engine roughness after takeoff at 2,000 feet, which continued after the instructor took control. The aircraft returned to the field and landed safely after reaching 4,600 feet.

ASRSN:2128213.n: Upon landing at ZZZ [runway] XL and slowing to exit the runway, brake pressure appeared to malfunction causing the DA40 to turn abruptly. FIight instructor procedurally took controls and was able to regain pressure and control the DA40.
ASRSN:2128213.s: A DA40 experienced a brake pressure malfunction while slowing to exit runway XL at ZZZ, causing an abrupt turn. The flight instructor took control, regained brake pressure, and safely controlled the aircraft.

ASRSN:2128216.n: My student and I departed ZZZ. A few minutes after departure, my student and I noticed the engine and had an abnormal vibration to it. I took controls of the airplane and advised ATC that we would like to return to the field just as a precaution. All engine instruments were reporting normal and the engine started to run normally once we turned base. ATC gave us a vector and we landed a few minutes later with no issues. After landing, the airplane was squawked and grounded for maintenance. No abnormal issues were observed during pre-flight and the run up did not indicate any abnormalities with the engine.
ASRSN:2128216.s: A pilot and student experienced abnormal engine vibration shortly after departing ZZZ, prompting a precautionary return. Although instruments remained normal and the vibration ceased before landing, the aircraft was grounded for maintenance post-arrival.

ASRSN:2128220.n: Climbout from ZZZ [airport] at XA02 local aircraft began to shudder and experience a drop in RPMs at 100% propellor load. IP (Flight Instructor) took controls and coms, with SP (Student Pilot) grabbing QRH and following the drop in RPM flow. Aircraft began a right bank and returned back to ZZZ [airport] without further incident after reducing power. Flight scheduled for XZ:30, aircraft X. On pre-flight walk around, noticed dark oil streaks down side of engine cowling. Reported to maintenance and squawked plane. Maintenance came to inspect engine and removed cowling for further inspection. They concluded that the oil on cowling was from someone pouring new oil into engine. This conclusion does not sit right with me because as you can see from the attached photos, the oil on the cowling is black while the oil we add to the engines is most definitely light golden in color. We know black oil must be oil that has been circulating in engine for some time and this is most definitely the oil that ended up on the cowling, not new oil. After noticing the oil on cowling, I checked to see if the oil cap was tightened properly, as stated in [our] safety bulletin - oil filler cap. The cap was tight enough that I had to twist hard to release it and it popped open once given enough force, definitely tight enough. This may have happened on a previous flight and the crew before us did not notice on pre-flight.During pre-flight I had read the maintenance logs and noticed multiple instances of engine roughness reported so the oil on cowling raised eyebrows extra high for me. Knowing the squawks, during the departure review, I briefed the squawks and the potential hazard. As on every other flight, during the departure review, after we briefed engine failure during takeoff roll and after liftoff actions, we established that in the event of power loss, engine failure or inflight event, my instructor will fly the aircraft and handle communications and I will fix (QRC, QRH actions).At the end of the before takeoff briefing, I mentioned the squawk again and mentioned how we should be on the lookout for signs of engine roughness and be ready for it to happen to us. IP replied that in the event it does happen we will pull the power back a bit to try and fix it and return to ZZZ [airport]. We performed a soft field takeoff from RWY XX and I brought the power up to 40% first, then moved it to max at a regular rate (not instantly pushing it to max as fast as possible). During takeoff roll I verified all instruments green and appropriate power and RPM's were being achieved. Upon reaching 420 feet MSL, I called 'flaps up' and as I reached over for the flap lever, I felt a distinct roughness in the engine. I immediately brought my hand back to the power lever and reduced power as I simultaneously pitched down so we wouldn't stall considering we were at 72 KIAS. I did this on instinct before I had time to look at the engine instruments to see if anything was out of limits because this is exactly what we had briefed during the takeoff briefing. After pulling the power back, the roughness continued for a few more seconds then went away on its own. Me and IP verbally agreed upon feeling the roughness and I contacted tower straight away and notified them that we would need to return to the airport. Tower instructed us to make right traffic at or below 1,500 feet, I replied with 'right traffic, Aircraft X'. After I replied to tower IP called 'my controls' I called 'your controls' and passed controls over to him. I pulled out the QRH while he flew the pattern and set us back up to land RWY XX. I read page 4-5 for excessive noise/vibration and verified auxiliary power off (the only action required). I then read propeller over speed on 4-6, knowing they just replaced the propeller governor, we hoped that maybe this would give us insight. However none of the actions applied to us as the engine appeared to be running normally. I then went to engine troubleshooting in flight on 4-4 and see if anything there would be applicable. By this time we were approximately mid right downwind and the aircraft seemed to be running appropriately so I discontinued the QRH actions.During this event, tower was telling traffic to delay inbound to give us space. We continued to make a normal landing and taxied back to the ramp without issue. IP squawked the plane.
ASRSN:2128220.s: A student pilot and flight instructor experienced engine roughness and RPM drop during climbout from ZZZ in aircraft X, likely due to pre-existing engine issues despite maintenance attributing oil streaks to new oil. The crew reduced power, returned to ZZZ, and landed safely after the roughness ceased.

ASRSN:2128231.n: Loss of braking at ZZZ [airport] in Aircraft X. Preflight and taxi brake check completed without any issues. Takeoff and landing for first four laps at ZZZ not an issue. Nothing out of the ordinary. Came in for a full stop taxi back, SP (student pilot) landed and got on brakes without any braking force, full to the floor. IP (Flight Instructor) took controls and co-pilot brakes went full to the floor. IP pumped the brakes, and left brake worked a little. Airplane started veering left at 50 KIAS ish. IP was unable to maintain directional control and slow down, so initiated go around. IP let go of brakes, and went full right rudder, rotated at 67 without running off the runway and departed via departure leg RWY XX. In the air, IP cycled parking brake, and pumped brakes multiple times on pilot and co-pilot side, still to the floor, but by the end had a little resistance. IP chose to return to ZZZ1 [airport] for a longer runway in case brakes were still fully failed. IP [advised ATC] inbound and landed full flaps on ZZZ1 RWY XY. IP had about 30% braking pressure upon landing, so could slow down, but not much resistance still. Taxied slowly to the ramp and shut down. IP squawked the plane.
ASRSN:2128231.s: A student pilot and flight instructor experienced total brake failure during a landing at ZZZ, forcing a go-around due to loss of directional control. They diverted to ZZZ1, landed with partial braking pressure, and the aircraft was subsequently grounded.

ASRSN:2128246.n: We were inflight at 3000 ft. north west and right outside ZZZ airspace when our right engine began to repeatedly drop RPMs with intermittent power loss. This repeated dropping of RPMs caused an asymmetrical thrust problem and threatened the controllability of the airplane. I was the PF and made the decision to fully secure the right engine after briefly troubleshooting the affected engine. Once secured and stabilized, the PM ran all of the appropriate checklist per request of the PF and the PF contacted ATC to inform them of an immediate return to ZZZ for landing on runway XX. The landing was safe and no damage to the runway environment or airplane was the result. The PF taxied the airplane back to the ramp on one engine and no services on the ground were required.
ASRSN:2128246.s: The pilot flying secured the right engine at 3,000 ft due to repeated RPM drops and power loss causing asymmetrical thrust. The crew returned safely to ZZZ for a landing on runway XX with no damage to the aircraft or environment.

ASRSN:2128279.n: While performing a circling maneuver to runway XX on the RNAV RWY approach into ZZZ, our aircraft experienced a near mid air collision with traffic departing from runway XX. Leading up to the incident, myself and the instructor I was with both made positions reports as we entered into the approach at the 10 mile, 5 mile, and 2 mile distance mark from the runway indicating our intentions to circle to runway XX on the RNAV approach. As we began circling to enter the pattern on a left downwind, the departing traffic from runway XX turned left crosswind directly into our flightpath. The indication on the G1000 showed the aircraft 200 ft below our position as we passed each other. Admittedly, in the heat of the moment as I neared minimums on the approach, I had missed hearing the departing aircraft's radio call, however, upon taking my foggles off and performing the circling maneuver, I was reassured by the instructor that the departing aircraft had indicated it would be turning in the opposite direction. Afterwards, once we determined the other aircraft had passed, we continued the maneuver to runway XX and then departed back to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:2128279.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced a near mid-air collision while circling to runway XX during an RNAV approach at ZZZ. The incident occurred when departing traffic turned left into their flightpath, passing 200 feet below, after the crew missed the departure's radio call and relied on incorrect instructor reassurance.

ASRSN:2128280.n: RNAV XX ZZZ, one engine simulated inoperative. LPV Amber alert prior to intercepting approach course, instructor/student decided to drop down to LNAV/VNAV minimums. We were fast on final, landing checklist was missed by both instructor and student. It was my fifth flight in the multi, turbulence was light to moderate. I felt task saturated trying to lower our speed, stay on glide path, stay on course, and get all the instrument callouts. Both instructor and student didn't notice the lack of landing gear until we were already in ground effect and I heard scraping.
ASRSN:2128280.s: During an RNAV approach with a simulated engine failure, an instructor and student missed the landing checklist due to task saturation. The aircraft landed with the gear up, resulting in scraping sounds upon entering ground effect.

ASRSN:2128294.n: Person A instructor, Person B student. We were in plane Aircraft X, we were being vectored for runway XXL. We were about a 3-4 mile final when the instructor saw a drone off the right side of the airplane. Drone was approx 300-500 ft agl. Drone was red, had no lights, and flying at a high rate of speed to the northwest directly on the approach flight path. Drone caused no deviations and caused no overall safety concerns with the airplane. Instructor reported the drone to tower.
ASRSN:2128294.s: An instructor and student in Aircraft X encountered a fast-moving, unlit red drone at 300–500 ft AGL while on final approach to runway XXL. The drone crossed the flight path but caused no deviations or safety concerns, and the instructor reported the incident to the tower.

ASRSN:2128303.n: My student and I were flying Aircraft X for his night lesson. We departed the runway 18 on runway heading on 88 KIAS and as soon as we hit 1,200 ft MSL and over hotels on the coastline, I spotted a flickering bright light approaching to us from the left side. I thought it was just a glare or reflection. Sooner, I noticed that it was a fast moving flying object and it was moving from the left to the right in front of our nose. It was less than 500 ft from us despite the degraded visibility at night, then I took the control and made a hard chandelle turn to the left to heading 120 degrees and informed MYR departure. After finishing the turn, I looked over my left shoulder and spotted the object flying over the approach lighting system and became lost from my vision. My student and I agreed that it was a drone. It was a little bit bigger than a basketball and was not a quad-copter based on the speed it was moving.
ASRSN:2128303.s: A flight instructor and student in Aircraft X encountered a suspected drone during a night departure climb at 1,200 ft MSL. The instructor executed a hard left turn to avoid the object, which passed within 500 feet before disappearing over the approach lighting system.

ASRSN:2128307.n: On departure from IND, Aircraft X was assigned runway heading 050 off runway 05R, then momentarily assigned 090 upon before reaching 2000ft MSL, departure controller assigned heading 140, where in a climbing right hand turn, Instructor onboard Aircraft X noticed a black object with blue lights, assumed to be a drone, 300-500ft to the left of the aircraft. Instructor reported the object to Indy Departure Controller. No evasive action was necessary and object passed below the aircraft.
ASRSN:2128307.s: During departure from IND, the instructor in Aircraft X observed a suspected drone 300-500 feet left while climbing on heading 140. The object passed below the aircraft without requiring evasive action after the instructor reported it to Indy Departure.

ASRSN:2128315.n: My student and I were at ZZZ alone in the pattern for Runway XX. We were doing a touch and go. Aircraft Y with other instructor pilot (IP) and other student pilot (SP) (private student), entered the pattern and proceeded to do a go-around. Due to their higher altitude and airspeed, allowing them to turn crosswind faster, they caught up to us in the downwind as we turned base. By the second pattern, Aircraft Y was within 0.5-0.75 miles of us according the ADS-B. We landed on the 1000 feet markers and as we touched down, the traffic alert sounded with +400 in yellow illuminating. When I looked behind my shoulder, they were in sight over the approach end of the runway. Aircraft Y called go-around soon after and flew right offset but even on the downwind they were still tailing us closely. I had to ask Aircraft Y to space themselves from us and on the third lap they chose to do a right 360 for spacing.
